description: The plot illustrates how accuracy (ACC) varies with co-occurrence number for six model editing techniques on Llama2. The x-axis is labeled “Co-occurrence Number” and uses a logarithmic scale, with major ticks shown at approximately 0, 10, 100, and 1000 and data points spanning from about 5 to about 3000. The y-axis is labeled “ACC (%)” on a linear scale, ranging from 60 to 85 with regularly spaced tick labels every 5 units. The Base series is a black solid line with circular markers, increasing from about 61.2 at the smallest co-occurrence to about 66.8 at the largest, with intermediate points near 63.5 and 65.1. FT is a blue solid line with downward-triangle markers, rising from about 62.3 to about 68.4 across the x-range (with points near 65.0 and 67.7 in between). IKE is a red solid line with upward-triangle markers, increasing from about 64.5 to about 70.1, passing through roughly 67.8 and 69.3. MEND is a brown solid line with diamond markers, moving from about 65.8 up to about 73.9, with intermediate values around 71.3 and 73.4. MEMIT is a purple solid line with pentagon markers, increasing from about 66.3 to about 72.6, with midpoints near 70.1 and 71.3. ROME is a green solid line with square markers, starting around 72.3 and rising to about 77.6, with intermediate points near 76.0 and 77.5 and a near-flat change between the last two x positions.
caption_used: The line plot depicts the performance of various model editing techniques on Llama2, measured by accuracy percentage (ACC) across an increasing number of co-occurrences. The x-axis, labeled 'Co-occurrence Number,' spans an exponential scale from 1 to over 1000, while the y-axis, labeled 'ACC (%),' ranges linearly from 60% to 80%. Six techniques are compared: Base (black, circular markers), FT (blue, downward triangles), IKE (red, upward triangles), MEND (brown, diamonds), MEMIT (purple, pentagons), and ROME (green, squares). The ROME method consistently outperforms all others, achieving an accuracy of approximately 77% at the highest co-occurrence value. The MEND and MEMIT techniques exhibit nearly identical performance, stabilizing around 70% accuracy beyond 100 co-occurrences. Notably, the FT method demonstrates a marked decline in accuracy after 100 co-occurrences, dropping to roughly 62% at the highest value. The Base method shows the least improvement, plateauing at around 66%. The IKE method, while initially competitive, is eventually surpassed by both MEND and MEMIT, finishing at just under 68%. Overall, the data reveal that advanced editing techniques like ROME and MEND yield superior and more stable performance across varying co-occurrence levels.
